note.note:
HISTORY AND PHYSICAL (H&P) NOTE

Patient: Jim Gowers  
DOB: 08 Aug 1958  
Encounter: Video visit – emergency triage  
Date/Time: [date/time not documented]

------------------------------------------------------------------
History:
• Chief complaint: Ongoing central chest pressure that began “a couple of hours” ago while kneeling to garden.  
• Character: Diffuse, heavy “like someone sitting on my chest.”  
• Radiation: Left arm and shoulder.  
• Associated symptoms: Shortness of breath, diaphoresis, mild nausea (no vomiting), awareness of faster heartbeat.  
• Severity/progression: Constant since onset; first ever episode.  
• Triggers/relief: Began with minimal exertion (light gardening); no relieving factors identified.  
• Prior episodes: None.  
• Social context: Lives alone; front door now open for EMS access.

Past Medical History:
• Hypertension.  
• No diabetes; cholesterol never checked.  
• Allergies: Aspirin – mild swelling reaction.  
• Medications: None documented.  
• Social: Smokes ~10 cigarettes/day x 15 yrs; drinks 7–8 pints beer/week; low physical activity; overweight.  
• Family: Father died of MI at ~60 y; mother with unspecified heart disease.

Physical Examination:
• General: Appears anxious, diaphoretic, short of breath on video.  
• Cardiovascular: Chest pressure reported; palpitations subjectively present. No objective exam possible via video.  
• Respiratory: Short of breath; no cough reported.  
• Neuro: Alert and oriented.  
• Abdomen/Extremities/Skin: Not recorded.  
• Vitals: Not recorded.

Impression:
Suspected Acute Coronary Syndrome (probable myocardial infarction) – classic pressure-type chest pain with left-arm radiation, diaphoresis, SOB, multiple CAD risk factors.

Top differential considerations consistent with transcript:  
1. Acute coronary syndrome – most likely.  
2. Aortic dissection – less typical presentation but hypertension/smoking risk; must rule out.  
3. Pulmonary embolism – dyspnoea/chest discomfort, though features less supportive.

Management Plan:
• Emergency services activated; ambulance en route.  
• Advise patient to remain seated near open front door; clinician staying on line until EMS arrival.  
• EMS to obtain 12-lead ECG and transport to nearest facility with cardiac capability.  
• Clinician to hand-off to EMS, including aspirin allergy details and need to weigh risk/benefit of antiplatelet therapy.  
• Hospital care to include cardiac enzymes, chest imaging, and definitive ACS management as indicated.  
• Reinforced importance of reporting aspirin allergy but understanding it may still be administered under monitored conditions.  
• No medications started via telehealth due to aspirin allergy and pending EMS evaluation.

Patient Summary:
60-year-old hypertensive, smoking male developed acute central chest pressure with left-arm radiation, nausea, diaphoresis, and dyspnoea while gardening. Presentation highly concerning for myocardial infarction; EMS dispatched for immediate evaluation and transport.

Key Takeaways:
• EMS is on the way—stay calm, seated, and keep the door unlocked.  
• Tell every provider you have an aspirin allergy (causes swelling).  
• Bring up smoking and blood-pressure history with hospital team; these impact treatment.

Next Steps:
• Pre-hospital ECG and cardiac monitoring.  
• Hospital work-up: serial troponins, ECGs, possible emergent cath lab activation.  
• Post-event: address risk factors—BP control, lipid profile, smoking cessation, weight management, alcohol moderation, structured exercise plan.

------------------------------------------------------------------
Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing elements: No vitals, medication list, comprehensive physical exam, problem list reconciliation.  
• Transcript/DDx conflicts: None noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear dialogue; no significant inaudible sections.
